name: Transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty

lead: In transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty the surgeon works through a cut on the inner surface of the lower eyelid, so there is no visible external scar. It removes or moves the fat that bulges as under-eye bags and smooths the lid-cheek transition, giving a flatter, less puffy under-eye once swelling settles.

Orbital fat is either removed or repositioned along the infraorbital rim to fill the tear trough hollow. It is an established technique in the plastic-surgery literature, including combinations with fat grafting; published support comes largely from surgeon case series.

paras: It is done under anaesthesia by a surgeon and suits people with fat bags and little or no excess skin. Where skin laxity is present, an additional procedure may be needed, and some surgeons add a canthopexy or canthoplasty.

Swelling and bruising are common and usually settle over several weeks. Eyelid malposition is a recognised complication of lower blepharoplasty in general. It is a surgical procedure that should be done by a qualified surgeon.

angle.text: Surgery through the inside of the lower lid removes or repositions under-eye fat for a flatter, less puffy lower lid, with no external scar. The visible change is the result itself once swelling settles.

lead: Transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty is lower-eyelid surgery in which the incision is made on the inner surface of the eyelid, leaving no external scar.[1] People have it to reduce under-eye bags, soften the tear trough hollow and smooth the transition between lower lid and cheek, which makes the eye area look less tired and the midface look fuller.[2][3]

A key feature of the technique is that orbital fat can be repositioned rather than only removed. The surgeon moves the herniated fat over the infraorbital rim to blend the lid-cheek junction and fill the tear trough.[2][3] Surgical reviews describe it as the treatment of choice when there is little lid laxity and visible fat pseudoherniation, while a skin incision just below the lashes is typically used when significant excess skin needs to be addressed.[2][4]

Reviewers highlight another advantage: working behind the eyelid may preserve the supporting function of the orbicularis muscle, which potentially lowers the risk of lower-lid retraction and ectropion.[4] Randomized trials and case series report outcomes for fat repositioning, fat grafting, laser versus electrosurgical incision and modified techniques that also address the tear trough ligament.[5][6][7][8]

paras: Lower blepharoplasty is generally performed by one of two routes. The transcutaneous approach uses an incision just below the lashes and permits skin excision, while the transconjunctival approach goes through the inner lid.[1] Orbital fat can be taken out or redistributed along the infraorbital rim to smooth the lower eyelid-cheek transition and address tear trough deformity.[1][2]

A 2016 review states that where a patient has little lid laxity and pseudoherniated periorbital fat, the transconjunctival route is the treatment of choice, because it lets the surgeon reposition fat and blend the lid-cheek junction.[2] A 2026 review argues for the approach in a broad range of patients, describing fat repositioning as preserving and redistributing orbital fat rather than simply excising it.[3] A review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics lists cosmetic and functional indications.[4]

Surgeons describe extended versions that release the tear trough ligament and redistribute fat,[9] retroseptal approaches combined with tear trough ligament and orbicularis retaining ligament release and orbital fat grafting,[7] and an enhanced method for intraorbital fat transposition and stabilization.[10] Another modification adds deframing and decompression maneuvers to the lower orbital fat compartment, aimed at an eye-opening effect on both upper and lower lids.[8]
Fat grafting and stromal vascular fraction (SVF) gel have also been used alone or with transconjunctival eye bag removal for tear trough deformity.[11]

A randomized trial of 78 patients compared carbon dioxide laser with monopolar electrosurgery for the transconjunctival incision, scoring bruising with an ecchymosis evaluation score. Patients reported more intraoperative heat sensation in the electrosurgery group.[6]

A prospective randomized study of 40 patients with fat prolapse and tear trough deformity compared a modified transconjunctival technique with traditional transconjunctival surgery plus orbital fat release, using tear trough classification and the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale as outcomes.[5] A prospective study of 80 eyes of 40 patients assessed retroseptal transconjunctival surgery with ligament release and orbital fat grafting for the groove in the infraorbital region.[7]

A report on 183 patients with four types of lower eyelid deformity in Asian patients described a combination of three-step lower blepharoplasty tailored to the deformity type, and a study of SVF-gel reported high patient satisfaction when used alone or with transconjunctival eye bag removal.[11][12] Many reports are surgeon-reported series.
Swelling and bruising are common after blepharoplasty and usually resolve over several weeks.[1] Canthopexy or canthoplasty may reduce the risk of postoperative eyelid malposition.[1]

A case report and systematic review described two cases of temporary orbicularis oculi palsy, with blink asymmetry, after transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty combined with radiofrequency-assisted liposuction; the review found an overall complication rate of about 5 percent for the face and neck for that adjunct procedure.[13]

Blepharoplasty has a long history: the first-century Roman writer Celsus described skin excision to relax the eyelids, and the term was coined by Karl Ferdinand von Graefe in 1818 for the repair of cancer-related eyelid defects.[1]
